Levitation is the act or phenomenon of a person, animal, or object rising and floating in the air — with no visible support holding it up, and apparently defying the force of gravity.

The key idea is this: normally, gravity pulls everything downward. Levitation is when something seems to escape that pull and hover above the ground, mid-air, without being held up by anything ordinary like a rope, a surface, or a hand.

Not every case of something being in the air qualifies as levitation. A bird flying is not levitation — it is actively using its wings to push itself through the air. A balloon floating is not levitation — it is being pushed upward by lighter-than-air gas. Levitation specifically implies a suspension or lift that has no immediately obvious mechanical explanation, or that works by a force that is not simple physical contact.

The word describes both the action (the process of rising and staying up) and the state (the condition of floating in mid-air).
Where You Will Encounter This Word

1. In Science and Technology

This is where levitation is most real and measurable.

Magnetic levitation (often shortened to "maglev") is the most well-known scientific form. Powerful magnets can create forces strong enough to push an object upward and hold it there, completely off the ground, with no physical contact. Maglev trains use this principle — they float above their tracks, which eliminates friction and allows them to travel at very high speeds.

Acoustic levitation is another genuine scientific phenomenon, where extremely powerful sound waves — too high-pitched for human ears to detect — create pressure zones in the air that can hold small, lightweight objects (like a droplet of liquid or a tiny bead) suspended in mid-air. Scientists use this in laboratories to study materials without letting them touch a surface, which can contaminate or alter them.

Electrostatic levitation uses electrical charge to suspend small objects. Objects with the same electrical charge repel each other, and this repulsion can be precisely controlled to hold things in mid-air.

In all these cases, something very real is doing the work — magnetism, sound, or electricity — but the result looks remarkable: an object floating with nothing visibly holding it up.

2. In Magic and Stage Illusions

Levitation is one of the most iconic and beloved acts in magic. When a magician performs levitation, they appear to make a person or object float — but this is, of course, an illusion. Cleverly hidden supports, mirrors, wires, and special rigging are used to create the impression that gravity has been overcome.

The famous "levitating assistant" trick, where a magician makes a person float horizontally in the air and then passes a hoop around them to "prove" nothing is holding them up, is a classic example. The audience knows it must be a trick, yet the visual effect is so powerful that it feels magical.

Levitation in this context refers to the performance and the illusion itself. You might say: "The magician's levitation act left the entire audience speechless."

3. In Spirituality, Religion, and Folklore

Across many cultures and religious traditions, levitation has long been associated with spiritual power, divine blessing, or supernatural ability. Certain saints in Christianity are said to have levitated during moments of deep prayer or religious ecstasy. In some Eastern spiritual traditions, advanced meditation or yogic practice is believed by some to enable the body to rise off the ground.

In folklore and supernatural stories, levitation is often a sign that a person has extraordinary or otherworldly powers — whether holy or sinister. Witches, for example, are popularly imagined as floating or flying, which is a form of levitation in the cultural imagination.

In these contexts, levitation is treated as a genuine, miraculous event, not an illusion or a trick — though whether such events actually occurred is a matter of personal belief rather than scientific evidence.

4. In Fiction, Fantasy, and Science Fiction

Levitation is extremely common in fictional storytelling. It is frequently portrayed as a superpower or magical ability that a character can consciously control — the ability to lift themselves or other objects into the air using their mind or magical force.

In superhero stories, a character might levitate as part of their power set. In fantasy novels or games, a wizard might cast a "levitation spell" to float across a chasm. In science fiction, advanced technology might allow a vehicle to levitate above the ground without wheels. Telekinesis — the fictional power to move objects with the mind — is closely related, and when it involves lifting something upward, levitation is the result.

Levitation is not always described as a dramatic, high-altitude event. The word applies whether something lifts a few millimetres off the ground or floats high above it. What matters is that contact with the ground or surface has been broken and the object or person is suspended in the air.

Levitation can also be brief or prolonged. A magnet might hold a small object levitated indefinitely. A stage illusion lasts a few minutes. A supernatural account might describe a saint levitating for seconds. The word works in all these cases.
How Levitation Is Used in Sentences

Here are examples that show the word in natural use across different contexts:

  • "The maglev train achieves levitation by using magnetic repulsion between the train and the track."
  • "The crowd gasped as the magician's levitation trick made his assistant appear to rise slowly into the air."
  • "Ancient texts describe the monk's levitation as a sign of his deep spiritual attainment."
  • "In the story, the wizard used levitation to carry heavy boulders across the river without touching them."
  • "Scientists used acoustic levitation to suspend a single water droplet in mid-air for study."

Knowing the related forms will make you more fluent with this word:

  • Levitate — the verb form. "The magnet caused the metal disc to levitate." / "She appeared to levitate above the stage."
  • Levitating — the present participle (used to describe something in the act of floating). "A levitating train."
  • Levitated — past tense. "The object levitated for several seconds."

Levitation is the word for floating or rising in the air against gravity, without ordinary support. Whether it happens through science (magnetism, sound waves), illusion (magic tricks), belief (spiritual accounts), or imagination (fiction), the word always carries that same central image: something that should be pulled to the ground is instead hovering, suspended, free of the earth beneath it.

That sense of impossibility — or at least of defying what seems natural — is what gives the word its power and why it appears in so many different areas of human life, from cutting-edge physics labs to ancient religious texts to Hollywood blockbusters.
